items.body: China And St. Augustine - Gavekal Research China And St. Augustine Louis-Vincent Gave Gavekal Research | 23 Oct 2026 Back in the summer of 2015, the Chinese government decided that equity markets had risen too far, too fast. The rug was pulled from under margin lending and various restrictions were put in place that brought the unfolding raging equity bull market to an abrupt end. By January 2024, the Chinese government reversed course and decided that Chinese equity prices had fallen far enough. Beijing intervened in the market (see Chinese Policies And Chinese Equities ) and put a floor under domestic markets. Equities duly rallied, delivering very solid returns for 2024 and 2025. However, over the past year, Chinese equity market returns have been fairly dismal. In fact, Chinese equity markets have now fallen for 10 consecutive weeks, a feat they had never achieved before. This in spite of the fact that (a) excitement over all things “artificial intelligence” has been a key driver of global equity market performance and that (b) China is one of the few countries outside of the US actually registering notable gains on the AI front. In short, Chinese equities have had a very disappointing month, quarter, year-to-date and 12 months and what had been steady outperformance has now melted away like snow in the sun. items.summary_en: Janet Zhou proposes funding civil-society overseers through stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments.
items.body: z_wei/Getty Images Who Pays the Fiscal Watchdogs? Oct 23, 2026 Janet Zhou Civil-society oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance, because it enables independent scrutiny long before a default. But given that a borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it, global decision-makers must do so using agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments. Listen to this commentary Please log in to listen to this commentary 0:00 / 0:00 Narrated by AI Audio unavailable HARARE—In 2021, Zimbabwean Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube caused an uproar when he issued more than $15 million in guarantees for private loans made by the Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe without seeking parliament’s approval. It was a particularly flagrant example of an unfortunately common practice in Zimbabwe: committing state resources to non-essential projects that offer no public benefit. Some of these loans invariably went unpaid, leaving taxpayers to cover the losses. In April 2022, the Zimbabwe Coalition on Debt and Development (which I led at the time), together with three co-applicants, petitioned the High Court of Zimbabwe to declare that parliament must approve public borrowing before it happens. In March 2023, the Court ordered the government to gazette a bill in the next 12 months outlining parliament’s role in approving loans and guarantees and establishing the procedure for ratification or rejection. This win was possible only because of a grant. The Open Society Initiative for Southern Africa, a regional foundation, funded the external lawyers who argued it, as well as our researchers, on a three-year cycle. When the cycle ended, the capacity to fight these legal battles went with it. This model of financing public accountability in developing countries through grants has started to collapse. Aid from OECD donors fell by 23.1% in real terms in 2025, the largest annual drop ever recorded. Meanwhile, governments are tightening the requirements for registering civil-society organizations and limiting which of these groups can receive funding from abroad. Zimbabwe’s Private Voluntary Organisations Amendment Act , enacted in April 2025, allows the authorities to cancel the registration of civil-society organizations and seize their assets without judicial oversight. El Salvador’s Foreign Agents Law , passed just one month later, imposed a 30% tax on all foreign funding. The weakening of civil-society participation will be felt widely, not least because every proposal for making global finance more sustainable and equitable depends on citizens who can read a debt-sustainability analysis and force a minister to answer for it. The Sevilla Commitment , adopted at last year’s Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, calls for strengthening parliamentary oversight of debt, independent audit institutions, and civil society’s role in exposing illicit financial flows. But nobody has said who pays for that work. The answer may lie in two types of international instruments: agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments. Each could contain a clause mandating that a fixed share of the sum—5% is a justifiable starting point—goes toward funding independent oversight of public finance in the recipient country. The money would be protected from executive interference, publicly audited, and guaranteed for the life of the program. items.title_en: What’s the Renminbi Got to Do With it? | Council on Foreign Relations
items.summary_en: A closer look at the impact of China’s currency on China’s export growth.
items.body: Council on Foreign Relations Articles By experts and staff Updated October 11, 2026 12:00 a.m. Brad W. Setser CFR Expert Whitney Shepardson Senior Fellow There is an argument—made in the recent Geneva Report and by various former IMF officials —that China’s current export surge is the simple consequence of the housing downturn and the resulting weakness in Chinese internal demand.* The weakness in the RMB in this story is entirely incidental to the increase in exports, which is, more or less, a mechanical response to weak internal demand. Cannot sell excavators at home? Export them. Built more modern car capacity than your internal market supports ? Export that too… The fall in the nominal RMB over the course of 2022 and the first half of 2023 in nominal and read terms was simply a function of domestic macroeconomic weakness, and a growing rate differential. It wasn’t an active policy choice by China’s central bank. Now, some might note that China’s currency doesn’t always move with rate differentials. The RMB didn’t consistently get pulled up when Chinese rates were higher than U.S. rates (2002-2020 generally speaking), and while it did fall when rate differentials moved against the RMB in 2022 and 2023, it then stabilized and has even appreciated modestly since the middle of last year. That appreciation hasn’t been big enough to correct the deep undervaluation of the RMB, but it came at a time when the PBOC policy rate (the reverse repo rate) was well below the U.S. policy rate. China doesn’t have an open financial account. As a result, equilibrium in the foreign exchange market is thus driven far more by exporter conversion and current account flows than by rate differentials and financial flows.** That, together with China’s ongoing management of the exchange rate and a trade surplus that can generate significant inflows, means that the value of the RMB is much more of a policy variable under the independent control of the Chinese authorities than a simple byproduct of monetary and fiscal policies. The modern IMF is reluctant to accept this conclusion. Its surveillance has generally ignored China’s currency management (even if that management is relatively obvious; see the data on FX settlement) and its recent comprehensive assessment of China’s economy completely ignored the balance of payments and exchange rate management. But it is pretty obvious to the market, even if the PBOC , rather absurdly , insists that “market forces play a decisive role in determining the RMB exchange rate.” I doubt the PBOC can win this argument. I agree with Mark Sobel : “The renminbi is still heavily managed and the authorities have acted to slow appreciation. The paper states that the PBoC phased out ‘regular’ foreign exchange intervention in 2017. But it has many means at its disposal to achieve the same effect through extensive capital controls, administrative guidance, signalling at the fix and deploying state-owned commercial banks. These means are heavily used. Thus, the word ‘regular’ must be taken with a pinch of salt . The comparison to Japan, which intervenes occasionally, is spurious – the yen largely floats freely in integrated global markets. The same cannot be said for the renminbi.” In reality, the PBOC’s daily fix now plays the decisive role in the currency’s path, and the market is often a bet on how the PBOC’s management of the yuan will evolve. That is clear from the lack of volatility in the yuan’s rate against the dollar. The yuan’s move down against the dollar in 2022 was a controlled 10 percent move, and the appreciation over the last 16 months has been even more controlled crawl. And the market is clearly massaged with substantial help from the state banks. In fact that the pattern of changes in the monthly FX settlement data looks exactly like the pattern of intervention of a central bank managing its currency around a tight band (the state banks in practice buy FX to keep the CNY from testing the strong side of the band, so there is an asymmetry in how the CNY is managed). None of this would matter much if China’s economy was small. But that obviously isn’t the case. Nor would this matter much if China’s exports didn’t respond to changes in the RMB’s real (and nominal) value. But that is also not the case. There is abundant evidence that China’s exports do respond to moves in the currency. Periods of RMB weakness have consistently been associated with periods of especially rapid Chinese export growth. Chancellor Merz and President Macron got this right, even if macroeconomic issues haven’t yet figured prominently in the EU’s dialogue with China.*** As they note in their open letter to the European Commission : “An appreciation of undervalued currencies towards a value more in line with fundamentals would help support the rebalancing of trade accounts with the EU in the short and medium term … European policy discussions focused on forging a common understanding of these exchange rate issues and their interaction with global imbalances would be useful.” The best evidence that exports responded to changes in the currency, and not simply to changes in the path of China’s internal demand, is the acceleration in China’s export growth after the RMB’s depreciation over the course of 2022. This is the killer chart. Now, you might ask: what of the acceleration in export growth in 2020 and 2021? That was pretty clearly tied to the global increase in goods demand that came with the pandemic and work from home requirements. It was expected to fade when the world economy normalized. But it didn’t. By 2023 Chinese export growth again topped global trade growth. The general expectation that the rise in China’s goods surplus during Covid would prove to be “transitory” heavily influenced the IMF’s work at the time: see the IMF’s external sector reports of 2023 and 2024 . Its effects were undermined, however, when Tokyo responded to the resulting slowdown with policies that exacerbated investment, credit expansion, and the very imbalances the adjustment was intended to resolve. Link Copied By Michael Pettis Published on Sep 25, 2026 In recent weeks and months there has been a resurgence in discussions in Europe and the United States about whether or not China should appreciate its currency in response to its enormous trade surpluses. As part of this discussion, analysts often point to the similarities between China today and Japan during the lead-up to the September 1985 Plaza Accord. In response to these discussions, however, Beijing has insisted that China will never tolerate a scenario where China plays the role once played by Japan. Last month, for example, former Chinese ambassador to the United States Cui Tiankai said , “I wish to advise people to give up the illusion that another Plaza Accord could be imposed on China. They should give up the illusion that China will ever give in to intimidation, coercion or groundless accusation.” Unfortunately, much of the discussion, including China’s response, is based on a very confused and highly politicized understanding of Japan’s economic performance in the 1990s and 2000s. The conventional account of the Plaza Accord—especially among China analysts—is that the United States forced Japan to accept a sharp appreciation of the yen, destroying Japanese export competitiveness, causing its economy to collapse, and eventually producing the Japanese “lost decades.” In this view, forcing a change in the value of the yen was a violation of Japanese sovereignty aimed at forcing Japan to give up its economic leadership. There are two problems with this interpretation. The first obvious problem is that for years Japan, along with Germany and other countries, had participated in exchange-rate policies and interventions that boosted the dollar’s value against their own currencies, contributing to a prolonged appreciation in the real value of the U.S. dollar that made American manufacturers far less competitive than their Japanese and European counterparts. The fact that Japanese intervention in the value of the U.S. dollar was not generally considered in Japan to be a violation of U.S. sovereignty, even as it undermined U.S. manufacturing, suggests that similar intervention from the other side should not have been considered a violation of Japanese sovereignty so much as a normal consequence of participation in the global trading system. A currency exchange rate, after all, does not belong to one country, but rather to that country and all of its trading partners. If the right to manipulate foreign currencies is symmetrical, this of course creates a parallel between Japan in the 1980s and China today, with the latter having actively intervened in the value of the U.S. dollar for decades, in ways that benefit its manufacturers while undermining those of the United States. Second, and more importantly, the problem with the conventional account of the Plaza Accord is that it gets the economic mechanism wrong. The Plaza Accord did not cause Japan’s long stagnation. Its purpose was to force an adjustment in the then-uneven distribution of global demand so that the manufacturing sectors of countries like Germany and Japan were no longer able to benefit from many years of weak domestic demand and wage suppression at the expense of their trade partners. By the mid-1980s, many Japanese and European policymakers recognized that the existing imbalances were unsustainable, but found it very difficult to reverse them. According to Japan’s own analysis, for example, the Japanese economy needed to transfer a greater share of total income to the household sector. This was most obvious from the famous report in 1986 by the Maekawa Commission, set up by former prime minister Nakasone Yasuhiro precisely to determine how Japan should respond to the international imbalances that had emerged. Resolving Japan’s Consumption Imbalance The report did not treat yen appreciation as an external punishment that Japan needed to resist. On the contrary, it argued that Japan had reached a point at which its postwar growth model had to be fundamentally changed. Japan’s current-account surplus had reached 3.6 percent of GNP in 1985, and the Maekawa Commission argued that the resulting external imbalance had reached a critical phase for Japan as well as for the international economy. Japan, it argued , needed a “historic” transformation away from an economy dependent on external demand and toward one led by domestic demand . The commission—and a growing number of Japanese economists and economic policy advisors—therefore called for a fundamental restructuring of Japan’s trade and industrial structure, greater imports and market access, more domestic consumption, better housing and urban development, reduced working hours, and higher disposable income. It also called for reducing the incentives that encouraged excessive household saving. The objective was to change the composition of Japanese demand and production. items.title_en: De-reservification, Not De-dollarization | Council on Foreign Relations
items.summary_en: The world isn’t moving away from the dollar. It is shifting its dollars from traditional reserves to state banks, pension funds, and other quasi-sovereign investors.
items.body: Council on Foreign Relations By experts and staff Published September 15, 2026 8:37 a.m. Brad W. Setser CFR Expert Whitney Shepardson Senior Fellow This is a joint blog with Alex Etra , Senior Macro Strategist and head of Flow of Funds at Vanda Research . The IMF’s data on the currency composition of foreign exchange (FX) reserves is scrutinized carefully for any signs that the world is shifting way from the dollar. Yet it doesn’t really matter that much if the dollar’s share of reserves has shifted from 56.5 percent to 57 percent. The ink-to-impact ratio of the quarterly reporting on the latest COFER data is all off. Neither the stock of global reserves nor the stock of dollar reserves has changed much in the last ten years. The action is elsewhere. China’s state banks (per the Bank of International Settlements) have almost as many foreign assets as the central bank (PBOC). Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) has almost as many foreign assets ( $986 billion ) as the government has FX reserves ($1.1 trillion at the end of August). Japan’s FX reserves are on the books of the Ministry of Finance and the GPIF is overseen by the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Labor—so these are almost all assets of the Government of Japan or the broader public sector, not its central bank. Korea’s National Pension Service has more foreign assets than the Bank of Korea has FX reserves. A different dynamic is in play in Taiwan, as the government doesn’t run a big retirement fund. But in a world where the hedge ratio of the life insurers has been (and still is) used as a policy tool, the shift in Taiwan’s foreign asset accumulation away from the Central Bank of China (CBC) and over to institutions whose activities in the foreign currency market it directly influences broadly fits into the same theme. So too does the PBOC’s use of the “macroprudential adjustment factor” effectively adjust banks’ net foreign assets in much the same way that CBC regulations adjust lifer hedge ratios. In the last year, the lifers’ hedge ratios—and their direct hedges with the central bank—have been one of the key tools the CBC has used to manage the Taiwan dollar (and guard the lifers’ solvency). Asia’s big surplus economies are in a sense just catching up with the world’s oil exporters. Norway put its oil surplus into a sovereign wealth fund from the start. Kuwait, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi (the most oil-rich emirate) all also have large sovereign funds. And the world’s biggest oil exporter has joined them: The Public Investment Fund has almost as many foreign assets as the Saudi Central Bank (SAMA).* What’s more, the available evidence suggests that the dollar share of these pools is in line with or higher than the dollar share of global FX reserves (it depends on the institution and jurisdiction). In other words, by looking at the (easily available) data on the world’s static holdings of formal FX reserve assets, scholars and analysts miss most of the growth in the world’s sovereign and quasi-sovereign foreign assets. Consider China. No serious analyst now disputes that China’s state banks—including the policy banks (the China Development Bank, China Exim)—hold several trillion in foreign assets . China reports $3.3 trillion in gross foreign assets to the BIS (the net position, counting foreign bank claims on the entire Chinese economy not just the banks, is $2.5 trillion). That maps to the BOP data, which shows almost $4 trillion in gross outflows through the banking system (technically, the sum of gross outflows in “other” plus the $500 billion in foreign currency bonds held by the state commercial banks) Since 2010 (and even more so after 2014) the net outflow through the state banks has exceeded reserve accumulation. The broad contours of this story are confirmed by the balance sheet data reported by state commercial banks in their 2025 annual reports, which showed that the top five banks held a combined $2.5 trillion in foreign currency assets (mostly held abroad). The Chinese haven’t disclosed the foreign assets of the two policy banks (with at this stage the complicity of the IMF, which has neither analyzed the role of SAFE policy bank financing, nor highlighted the glaring gap in China’s own reporting). But the work of AidData points to nearly $1 trillion in foreign assets, with a hefty dollar share. The available data sources all suggest that the bulk of the foreign assets of the state banks are in dollars. SAFE’s disclosure—which covers the commercial banks—puts the dollar share of their offshore foreign currency assets at around 70 percent. That is well above the last disclosed dollar share of China’s formal reserves (55 percent in 2019). The banks’ annual reports suggest that about 70 percent of the banks’ assets are in dollars and Hong Kong dollars (55 percent USD/15 percent HKD)—a bit below the dollar and Hong Kong dollar share of their liabilities (swaps out of the HKD fund a decent share of the banks euro assets). Put simply, SAFE’s static dollar holdings aren’t the important story. The real story is the rapid growth of the state banks dollar holdings . Japan holds a high (though undisclosed) dollar share in its FX reserves, and those reserves are primarily invested in Treasuries—so Japan’s MoF is now clearly the largest contributor to the U.S. data on foreign official holdings of Treasuries. ( SAFE has shifted its funds out of U.S. custodians , and thus increasingly appears in the data as a “private” holder in a European custodial center) Japan’s formal reserves haven’t changed much in the last ten years; periodic sales to limit the yen’s weakness have offset most of the MoF’s accumulated interest income. China’s banking crisis in the 2000s was resolved by transferring the costs to households through financial repression—a decision that recapitalized the banks while exacerbating the structural imbalances that continue to shape the Chinese economy today. Link Copied By Michael Pettis Published on Aug 25, 2026 Chinese debt has risen over the past ten to fifteen years at perhaps the fastest pace in history, leaving China with one of the highest debt-to-GDP ratios in the world—second only to Japan among the major economies. What is more, surging debt has always been the warning for investment-driven “miracle” economies that their growth model has become unsustainable. That is why it is not surprising that analysts have become increasingly concerned about how China will ultimately resolve its debt burden. Some look back to the cleanup of China’s banking system in the early 2000s, following the explosion of bad lending during the 1990s, as a possible model for dealing with today’s debt overhang. Unfortunately, they often draw the wrong lesson, seeing the experience of the 2000s as suggesting that China can resolve a banking and debt problem at little cost to the economy. But in fact, the cleanup was extraordinarily costly, and shaped the Chinese economy in ways that are discussed almost daily today in the Chinese press. The way Beijing chose to resolve its debt burden laid the foundations for many of the deepest structural imbalances in China’s economy over the subsequent two decades. For that reason, it is worth reconsidering how China resolved its debt problems in the 2000s. The original problem emerged in the 1990s, when banks functioned primarily as quasi-fiscal institutions supporting state-owned enterprises (SOEs), local governments, and industrial policy, rather than allocating capital on commercial terms. Credit allocation was largely administrative, as it had been throughout the four decades since the founding of the People’s Republic. Loans were extended because enterprises were politically important, because local governments wanted investment, or because employment had to be maintained, and rarely because the projects they funded were expected to generate adequate returns. The way Beijing chose to resolve its debt burden laid the foundations for many of the deepest structural imbalances in China’s economy. Many of these loans were, in effect, fiscal transfers disguised as bank credit, and in many ways, this remains one of the primary functions of China’s banking system today. As a result, the largest source of bad debt was lending to SOEs. Many SOEs remained grossly inefficient, with excess employment maintained for reasons of social stability even as prices were liberalized, competition intensified, and profitability collapsed. Yet banks continued lending because allowing widespread bankruptcies was politically unacceptable. By the late 1990s, China’s banking system was burdened with enormous quantities of non-performing loans. The Big Four state-owned banks—which accounted for the overwhelming majority of commercial bank lending—were technically insolvent. Official estimates suggested that roughly 25 to 30 percent of their loan portfolios were non-performing, while many independent analysts, including the World Bank, believed the true figure was closer to 40 or 50 percent. Rural credit cooperatives and many local banks were widely believed to have even higher proportions of non-performing loans. 1 As Beijing prepared for World Trade Organization (WTO) accession and sought both to modernize and partially to privatize its banking system, policymakers recognized that banks burdened with such large volumes of bad loans would be extremely difficult to sell, especially to the foreign strategic investors they hoped to attract. The decision was therefore made to recapitalize the banks before listing them on the Hong Kong and Shanghai stock exchanges. As part of this process, Beijing transferred bad loans from the Big Four banks to newly created asset-management companies (AMCs), injected fresh capital into the banks, strengthened regulation and accounting standards, and brought in foreign strategic investors. 2 At the time, many economists assumed the cleanup would be largely technical. Bad loans would be transferred, banks recapitalized, accounting standards improved, and the banks successfully listed. That is broadly what happened. What was much less widely understood was who ultimately paid for the most important—and by far the most expensive—part of the reform: the bad loans themselves. Every Banking Crisis Is Ultimately About Loss Allocation What is often forgotten in discussions of banking crises is that every bad-debt resolution is fundamentally a question of loss allocation. When the value of an entity’s assets falls below the value of its liabilities, someone must absorb the resulting loss. Normally, the first losses fall on the owners through lower equity values. If those losses exceed the owners’ equity, creditors typically absorb the remainder. But when the owners or creditors are politically powerful—or when imposing losses on them threatens broader financial stability—governments often intervene to socialize the losses instead. There are many ways to do this, but in almost every case the losses are ultimately transferred, often indirectly, to the household sector. items.title_en: As Europe Dithers, the Cost of Derisking from China Rises
items.summary_en: The cost of confronting China will be high. But the cost of waiting—for Europe’s economy, security, and sovereignty—could be far higher.
items.body: In March 2023, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called on Europe to unite behind a policy of economic derisking from China. In a speech in Brussels, she warned about Europe’s deepening dependencies on Chinese rare earths, called for more robust trade measures to protect European industry from unfair competition and for new tools to restrict the flow of sensitive technologies to China. More than two and a half years later, it is clear that her warning has gone largely unheeded. Today, Europe is more dependent on critical inputs from China than ever before. China’s export restrictions on critical minerals and chips produced by the Chinese-owned Dutch firm Nexperia have hit European companies in the auto, medical, and defense sectors in recent months, laying bare Europe’s failure to derisk. EU trade defense instruments cover less than 10% of imports from China despite evidence of systemic state support for Chinese companies and an economic model that has relied for years on flooding global markets with cheap goods . Efforts to restrict the flow of artificial intelligence, quantum, and chip technologies to China have stalled amid resistance from European member states. There are many reasons for this failure. The EU has been consumed by more urgent crises, from Russia’s war in Ukraine to Donald Trump’s trade war. It is a bloc of 27 countries in which policy consensus can be slow and painful. New regulatory instruments can take years to put in place, and when they finally arrive, there is often resistance to deploying them with full force. The bloc’s anti-coercion instrument, for example, has been sitting idle at a time when Europe has been subject to economic coercion on an unprecedented scale—both from China and the United States. The longer tackling the derisking challenge is delayed, the harder and more expensive it becomes. But this caution has come at a high cost. Every day that action to protect European workers from cheap, subsidized Chinese competitors is delayed, the EU loses an estimated 500 manufacturing jobs. With every month that passes, China’s trade surplus with Europe widens by 7 billion euros compared to the previous year. Every quarter, European wind companies lose 1% of their global market share to Chinese counterparts, increasing the risk that these firms go bust and that Europe’s dependence on Chinese renewable technologies deepens. Every year, China exports one million more cars—almost equal to France’s annual automotive production—even though global demand for autos is flat. The effect is to destroy production capacity elsewhere. The longer tackling the derisking challenge is delayed, the harder and more expensive it becomes. In the two years since von der Leyen gave her speech in Brussels, China has increased its share of the so-called “legacy chips” market (in which Nexperia operates) from 32% to 40%, laying the ground for the next major China dependency in Europe and the West. Over the past four years, China’s share of refined cobalt production has risen from 65% to close to 80%, further entrenching Europe’s reliance on China for a core input in energy and defense supply chains. The idea for an ambitious project to open Europe’s first rare earths magnet recycling and refining plant in the southwest of France was first floated in 2020. But it didn’t secure the necessary financing from French and Japanese government-backed sources until this year. Commercial output of heavy rare earth magnets will only begin in 2027, leaving Europe at the mercy of China’s export controls. While Chinese authorities have been openly pursuing a policy to reduce their country’s dependence on the rest of the world and increase the reliance of others on China, Europe has been busy writing new strategies, conducting risk assessments, establishing task forces and launching expert commissions to assess how Europe should respond. These initiatives, no matter how well-intended they are, have become damaging distractions because they are not producing concrete results—at least not any that measure up to the size of the challenge. They create the illusion of action, when too little of that has taken place. Europe, despite the best efforts of leaders in Brussels, is wasting time. It is clear by now that the bloc needs to be much nimbler and bolder in responding to the economic risks emanating from China. How could this be achieved? First, member states could decide to transfer more powers to the Commission in a range of security-related policy areas, from investment screening and conditioning, to export controls, and cybersecurity. Second, EU processes could be accelerated through a greater reliance on emergency procedures or provisional trade measures. The bloc’s response to the euro financial crisis, COVID-19 pandemic, and Russian invasion of Ukraine provide a blueprint. Third, where EU-27 consensus is not possible, big member states could decide to build coalitions of the willing, pressing ahead with policies and inviting others to follow. Fourth, the EU could dust off its dormant anti-coercion instrument to take more drastic measures against China, using Beijing’s export controls on critical raw materials and chips as a trigger. All of this will require political leadership in European capitals, from Berlin and Paris to The Hague, Warsaw, and Rome. The cost of confronting China will be high. But the cost of waiting—for Europe’s economy, security, and sovereignty—could be far higher. Share X LinkedIn Bluesky Email Practice Area China Topics Policymaking and reform​

news_items.title_en: Novel idea: Thailand, Vietnam take books on the road in reading drive | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Two independent publishers travel through regional provinces, offering discounted titles to spark curiosity and connect local communities.
news_items.body: Tran Dai Thang spotted two young people who had picked up their drinks at a pop-up cafe beside his travelling bookstore and were about to leave, so he called them over. One of them said they did not read books, Thang recalled. But he kept the conversation going and eventually persuaded the visitor to buy a book for 10,000 dong (US$0.40) – heavily discounted from its original price of 45,000 dong. For Thang, an artist and publisher, the small sale mattered far less than the fact that someone who said they did not read had chosen to pick up a book. “Who knows, it might be the start of a new habit,” he said. Thang, 53, is spending a year travelling across Vietnam in a truck with his “Books To Every Home” project, also known as “Roaming Turtle”. In neighbouring Thailand, a similar book truck named “Somelee” (Cotton) is pursuing an equally ambitious mission: visiting all 77 provinces to take literature beyond Bangkok and the country’s other urban centres. Their goal goes beyond selling books. By taking their trucks beyond the big cities, the two projects hope to spark curiosity, build connections through storytelling and turn chance roadside encounters into lasting reading habits for people who might otherwise never enter a bookshop. But bringing books to the provinces comes at a cost – from fuel and accommodation to staff wages – and neither truck can guarantee a crowd at every stop. ‘Come with me for a year’ Thang’s decision to start Roaming Turtle followed the closure of the last branch of his Ca Chep bookshop chain on Ho Chi Minh City’s Vo Van Tan Street in June. Customers were increasingly buying online, he said, and he no longer had the time or focus to run the store. As its closure approached, a former employee offered to help him sell books. “Then come with me for a year,” Thang recalled replying. With no advance plan, the truck set off on July 15 from Ho Chi Minh City on a journey scheduled to last until July 2027. By mid-October, Thang said the Roaming Turtle had reached its 27th stop – Nam Dinh in the Red River Delta – with Thai Binh next on the itinerary. “The Ca Chep Bookstore may have closed its fixed location, but we don’t want the story of Ca Chep to end there,” he said, noting that Ca Chep means carp in Vietnamese. “Ca Chep only temporarily paused, but never stopped swimming.” Growing up in mountainous Hoa Binh province, Thang loved reading and drawing. After graduating from the University of Industrial Fine Arts in 1995, he designed book covers at a state-owned publisher before establishing Dong A, his own book company. On the road, those skills come together. Together with a driver and a sales assistant, Thang introduces readers to Dong A’s titles and hand-draws book covers upon request. Bystanders even help unload boxes, arrange displays and manage sales. His autobiography has become a particular attraction. He initially brought five copies to sell at each stop, illustrating every cover differently. When those sold out, readers began ordering copies online and bringing them to his truck to be illustrated. In Da Nang, he hand-illustrated 22 covers. “Each book cover is a unique illustration, connected to a person and a memory from my journey,” he said. Other encounters have triggered deeper personal memories. In Quy Nhon, he met an unemployed mother who used her limited savings to buy books for her child – a scene that reminded him of his own childhood and mother. Beyond the capital In Thailand, the team behind the Somelee book truck began with a similar problem of access. Bookshops and literary fairs were concentrated in Bangkok and other major urban centres, according to Yasawath Chuthivisitrathikul, a project manager at P.S. Publishing. The publisher was previously affiliated with Somewhere Bookshop and Home Cafe in Bangkok’s Yai district, which closed its doors on Sunday. “We saw this as an opportunity to reach everyone – both readers and people who have never read books before,” Yasawath said. news_items.summary_en: ‘I don’t know how much longer I can do this,’ says the stand-up comedian, fresh off three sold-out Hong Kong shows. Is he joking?
news_items.body: “I think about quitting all the time,” says Jordan Leung, known to his Instagram followers as @69ranch. As one of Hong Kong’s most prominent stand-up comedians to emerge in recent years, Leung’s pessimism is surprising. “I don’t wanna make social media content,” the 33-year-old admits. “Now I’m just fixated on likes and stuff … I don’t know how much longer I can do this.” Sitting directly across the table from him, it is not always easy to tell when Leung is being sincere or performing his deadpan jesting – yet, at this moment, his exhaustion sounds genuine. Leung recently returned to Hong Kong from his base in New York, taking a couple of weeks to spend time with family and recover from jet lag ahead of his “Back to Work” tour shows in Whampoa in October. Originally planning to perform one show each in English and Cantonese on October 17 and 18, the comedian added an extra Cantonese show on the final day thanks to overwhelming demand. At his English-language performance, Leung was his usual understated character: clad in black and sporting his signature thick moustache, delivering monotone observations on the bizarre experiences of his daily life. His set included stories of being hit on by a billionaire’s daughter after a gig, childhood memories of realising his uncle is gay and the challenges of touring Japan. He also touched on his life as a full-time stand-up comedian, joking that his mother would have sought an abortion if she had known this was his career choice. Ironically, during our interview, Leung reveals that since finding success in comedy, his parents insist he cannot quit. “‘You’ve spent too much time on this,’” he quotes them. A comedy career pivot Leung grew up in Hong Kong before moving to the United States at 15, then returned to the city in 2020 after getting laid off from a tech job. He has toyed with stand-up comedy since he was 23, taking classes at New York’s renowned Comedy Cellar and performing bar gigs as early as 2017. He always knew he would quit tech and pursue something more creative once he saved enough money anyway. “I knew there was a comedy scene here [in Hong Kong], and I knew I would be able to produce some shows, but I just never imagined the scale that it would eventually become,” Leung says. “But that was probably one of the most important things I did in my career.” He built a significant following through viral Instagram videos making jokes about Hong Kong life using bawdy humour, often amassing hundreds of thousands of views. Eventually, he even held shows at MacPherson Stadium in Mong Kok in 2024. Then, in 2025, Leung returned to the US. His live sets often feature jokes that lean into Asia diaspora experiences, such as learning Hong Kong slang words for intimate body parts. At his recent English live show, Leung delivered several jokes about female genitalia seemingly aimed at a much younger audience than the crowd of 30- and 40-year-olds present – but the crowd guffawed, nonetheless. The response was mixed for a particular joke deriding Shenzhen, with roaring laughter and booing from the audience alike. The gag was in vein with much of his set: “edgy” but not countercultural. Some of the funniest moments came when he switched to Cantonese to make small quips and quick jabs. However, his crowd work segment – which lasted only a few minutes – hit an unfortunate lull when audience members seemed reluctant to engage, and the interactions quickly devolved into an awkward back-and-forth. Suffering backlash Leung’s penchant for gags has brought its own fallout. Following his Cantonese show on October 18, controversy erupted over his opening act, Taiwanese-Hong Kong comedian Shen Jong, whose set included an offensive joke about the benefits of sleeping with female cancer patients. news_items.title_en: Will China’s 4 peace principles for tackling African conflicts work? | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Beijing seeks to safeguard billions in regional infrastructure and economic investments while hewing to its pledge of non-interference.
news_items.body: Beijing has a formula for tackling African conflicts and hot-button issues, and during a meeting this month with Togolese leader Faure Gnassingbe, Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined it in four principles linking peace to development. The principles entail focusing on African-led security free from outside intervention; upholding sovereignty and UN Charter principles; rejecting force and sanctions and favouring ceasefires through dialogue; and focusing on both immediate security concerns and long-term development. Asked on Monday whether the principles could be applied to northern Ethiopia and heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said they offered “practical guidance” for the Horn of Africa. Days later, a joint statement following a meeting between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Djiboutian counterpart, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, said China would continue to play a constructive role in mediating regional disputes through its existing Horn of Africa peace-and-development initiative, subject to the wishes of the countries concerned. Beijing has financed major infrastructure projects in the region under the Belt and Road Initiative, its China-centred trade and investment scheme. These include the Addis Ababa–Djibouti Standard Gauge Railway, as well as oil, fishing and maritime interests across Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and Djibouti. Yet, Beijing remains reluctant to intervene directly, opting instead to support African-led diplomacy to preserve its long-standing doctrine of state non-interference. As conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region threatens to destabilise the Horn of Africa, China seeks to strike a delicate diplomatic balance advocating for peaceful, African-led solutions that align with Xi’s conflict-resolution principles. The idea is to safeguard China’s billions in regional infrastructure and economic investments while carefully maintaining its core foreign policy pledge of non-interference. But experts said lasting peace would ultimately depend on regional actors addressing internal factionalism, respecting state sovereignty and fostering inclusive dialogue alongside broader international peace efforts. Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China programme at the Stimson Centre, a Washington-based think tank, said Beijing’s response reflected concern about what renewed fighting could mean for its interests in the Horn of Africa. “I think it first and foremost points out China’s concern and aversion to instability,” Sun said. “War and conflicts fundamentally undermine China’s interests on the ground.” China also faced a diplomatic constraint, she added, saying it seeks to influence how conflicts are resolved without abandoning its stated principle of non-interference in other countries’ affairs. Rather than lead a peace process itself, Beijing tends to support approaches led by countries in the region and their regional organisations. “The balance they strike is through siding [with] and supporting [a] regional approach and the involvement of regional organisations,” Sun said. “That confers legitimacy and credibility to the Chinese approach.” Ethiopian federal forces and fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) are battling again in northern Ethiopia, putting the 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement under severe strain. Ethiopian federal forces entered Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, in early October after advancing on the city and prompting TPLF fighters to withdraw. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government announced a six-month caretaker administration in the Tigray region to restore services, return displaced people and prepare for elections. The conflict has also escalated Ethiopia–Eritrea tensions, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of backing the TPLF and occupying its territory. news_items.summary_en: Smart coolers offer seamless grab-and-go convenience but local operators say city’s distinct economic factors may stall widespread adoption.
news_items.body: Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan. The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the only time she spends is deciding what to buy. The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it. “I buy things basically every day … I can grab multiple items at once after just opening the door,” she said. “The open-door machines are more convenient because you do not have to wait for items to drop one by one from traditional machines that sometimes get stuck.” For decades, vending machines have evolved from simple dispensers of bottled or canned drinks into smart retail points that combine digital payments and data-driven consumer insights. They now offer a low-cost retail channel for third parties such as local charities, selling products like flowers and daily necessities – from disposable underwear to sanitary towels. These artificial intelligence-powered open-door vending machines have been growing in popularity in Shenzhen in the past couple of years, but they remain a minority in Hong Kong. Some operators have pledged to install more of them across the city in the coming months, with one reporting higher sales revenue during the trial stage. IVM Technology is one of Hong Kong’s largest operators, managing around 800 AI vending machines alongside 1,500 traditional ones in Hong Kong, the firm’s founder and managing director Leo Lui told the South China Morning Post. Hong Kong currently has an estimated 15,000 to 17,000 vending machines, with the number expected to increase as the lower capital costs of AI machines attract new market entrants, Lui said. “It will not surprise me if there are 30,000 to 40,000 machines later,” he said. Lui pointed to Hong Kong’s exorbitant logistics, labour and parking costs – such as paying HK$200 just to park a delivery van for restocking at major commercial sites – as a major bottleneck. Unlike mainland Chinese operators who could rely on low delivery expenses to sell low-margin goods, Hong Kong vending businesses faced fixed transport costs of about HK$2 per item, forcing them to focus on higher-priced, premium inventory, Lui said. news_items.summary_en: Even as the region’s economic downturn is expected to worsen, Gulf states are slated to spend tens of billions of dollars on infrastructure.
news_items.body: Before the outbreak of the war triggered by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, the Gulf monarchies were living the prosperity dream that was the envy of the world. Their hydrocarbon-fuelled economies were glitzy oases of growth, inoculated from the conflict in Gaza that had rocked other parts of the Middle East for several years. Underpinned by decades-old US security guarantees and conflict mediation by billionaire sheikhs, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar cultivated images as peaceful lands of opportunity as they invested staggering amounts of money in economic diversification programmes. Backed by sovereign wealth funds with trillions of dollars invested mostly in the West, these leading states of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) embarked on transformative programmes to reposition their economies amid the global transition away from oil and gas. Similar diversification initiatives were also happening in Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain, the other three GCC members. Such a shift towards long-term economic stability is important in maintaining the political legitimacy of the Gulf monarchies in the eyes of their burgeoning young populations, especially amid mounting public anger at the carnage in Gaza, according to analysts. The GCC states, as well as other Muslim-majority governments such as Pakistan and Turkey, eventually persuaded US President Donald Trump to end the Gaza war in October 2025, renewing optimism about the Gulf economies. However, everything changed soon after the Gaza ceasefire, when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu managed to convince Trump to go to war against Iran. Rather than just retaliating against Israel, Iran has also vented its fury against the GCC states, attacking energy infrastructure, airports and ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. With Trump weighing his options, including both another military escalation and a politically inconclusive end to the war with Iran after midterm congressional elections on November 5, uncertainty reigns in the Gulf region. The eruption of war between Saudi Arabia and Tehran’s Houthi rebel allies in Yemen last month has exacerbated these anxieties. Driven by necessity, GCC governments have unveiled plans to stabilise their economies. The two largest in the bloc – Saudi Arabia and the UAE – are on the verge of a potential technical recession caused by the Iran war, while Qatar is already in a recession. In the second quarter of this year, Saudi Arabia’s economy – the largest in the GCC – fell by 4.8 per cent from 3 per cent growth in the first quarter. The UAE’s economy – the Gulf’s logistical hub – decreased by 2.1 per cent from an expansion of 3 per cent over the same period. Qatar’s economic outlook worsened, with its GDP declining by 15.7 per cent in the second quarter, accelerating from a drop of 7 per cent in the first quarter. According to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) projections published on October 13, the UAE is expected to record a 3.9 per cent drop in its GDP in 2026 from a pre-war forecast of 3.1 per cent growth, while Saudi Arabia is projected to fall by 3.3 per cent this year from an earlier predicted 4.6 per cent growth. Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are set to record double-digit GDP contractions in 2026. Like the IMF, the World Bank has forecast the GCC economies to rebound in 2027 if hostilities end this year and unhindered passage through the Strait of Hormuz is restored by next March. news_items.title_en: Singapore tells suppliers to ‘honour commitments’ amid Indonesia’s gas cut | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the government would explore nuclear power and boost global partnerships for energy security.
news_items.body: Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports. Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests. Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to less than 2 per cent of Singapore’s total daily gas demand. About 95 per cent of Singapore’s electricity is generated using natural gas and it imports a significant amount of this gas through pipelines from Indonesia. “The gas supplies are covered by commercial contracts. We expect all parties to honour their commitments and Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under these contracts,” Wong said. Singapore has been readying itself for such risks, the prime minister added. It has invested in liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals to import natural gas from different countries, without having to rely on pipelines, providing more options to manage any disruptions to supply. However, Singapore must look beyond natural gas to cleaner sources of power that can provide reliable electricity around the clock, Wong added. This is why authorities are studying the potential of nuclear energy, he said. “Understandably, there are concerns about the safety of nuclear power in a small and densely populated country like Singapore. We take the concerns very seriously. Safety must come first,” Wong said. “But we should not rule out an option simply because it is difficult or controversial. We must assess the risks and trade-offs carefully, engage Singaporeans, and eventually make the right decision to secure our energy future.” From 2027, Singapore will be embarking on an assessment by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to gauge the country’s ability to make an informed decision on adopting nuclear energy. Known as the IAEA’s Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review, each phase comes with key milestones that have to be reached to guide countries in their understanding of the commitments and obligations associated with developing a nuclear power programme. Wong said: “Dealing with today’s concerns is only part of our job. It will still be driven by ideas and talent, but computing power will become increasingly important and that requires enormous amounts of energy.” In his speech, Wong noted that the world has become more “dangerous and troubled”, with harder challenges, but Singapore faces these difficulties from a position of strength, he added. “We remain a trusted partner and an attractive place for businesses and investors,” the prime minister said. news_items.title_en: ‘Mum, good’: Chinese woman wakes vegetative daughter-in-law after 17 years of care | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Xuan feeds Xu liquid food spoonful by spoonful, taking an hour per meal, and turns her over 10 times daily to prevent bedsores.
news_items.body: A woman in eastern China has been devotedly caring for her daughter-in-law for 17 years, ever since she fell into a vegetative state, moving social media users. The younger woman, surnamed Xu, fell into a vegetative state in 2009 after being struck by a truck in her village in Qingyun county, Shandong province. The accident happened just one month after she got married, Shandian News reported. Since then, her mother-in-law, Xuan Fengying, has cared for her around the clock. “She married my son, so she’s my child. How could I abandon her?” the 68-year-old Xuan was quoted as saying. Xuan fed Xu liquid food one spoonful at a time, and each meal took an hour. She also helped Xu turn over more than 10 times a day to prevent bedsores. Other caregiving tasks included washing Xu after she became incontinent and regularly massaging her muscles. Xuan also talked to Xu about news from the family and their village, played her favourite songs, and repeatedly called her name. Several years ago, Xu miraculously emerged from the vegetative state. Her mother-in-law continued to care for her, as severe brain damage from the accident had left Xu with the cognitive abilities of a four-year-old. Xuan helped Xu learn to walk and take part in other rehabilitation exercises. Xu can now speak a few words and even cook simple meals on her own. “Mum, good,” Xu was filmed saying to her mother-in-law. “I have no other wish than for her to keep getting better. I feel a little relieved that she can cook. That way, after I pass away, she’ll still have something to eat,” Xuan said. “I told my son that if I pass away, he should keep caring for his wife,” Xuan added. She said her legs had ached for years and that she had high blood pressure. Xuan recalled that when Xu once fell to the ground, she had to ask a neighbour to help her get Xu back up. “Of course I envy other people’s leisurely lives. They can go dancing in the squares. But my responsibility is to care for my daughter-in-law,” Xuan said. A flood of comments followed, with many people moved by Xuan’s extraordinary devotion. “Such great maternal love! Salute to this mother-in-law,” one social media user wrote. Another commented: “Wishing this elderly woman good health and a long life.” Stories of people devoting many years to caring for family members often make headlines in China. Earlier this year, a husband in central China’s Henan province won widespread praise online for caring for his severely paraplegic wife for 25 years.

news_items.summary_en: For many on the mainland, the recent rising sun flag incident and controversies like it show a fondness for anime and manga only goes so far.
news_items.body: Young Chinese people enjoy Japanese pop culture such as anime and music, but many draw a firm line at symbols of Japanese militarism. That line was tested recently at Moscow State University, where Chinese students confronted a classmate wearing Japan’s rising sun flag in class and called for his repatriation, state-run newspaper Global Times reported on Sunday. Many countries, including China, view the flag as a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression. Japan’s Self-Defence Forces still use the flag today. The October 14 incident sparked an online backlash against the Chinese student and praise for those who reported him, following commentaries by People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s official newspaper, and the People’s Liberation Army. “A disgrace to the Chinese people,” read one of the top comments under a post by Jun Zhengping, a social media account run by the PLA. The Japanese anime fan began watching the medium in primary school, watching more than 200 anime series and reading manga – Japanese comic books and graphic novels. “Japan in anime cannot really be called Japan but is an idealised utopia,” Huang said, adding that she drew a clear distinction between Japan in reality and the country as depicted in anime. She said it was “unforgivable” for a Chinese person to wear the rising sun flag. Japanese anime began appearing on Chinese television in the 1980s and gradually gained a larger audience over the following decades. According to a 2018 report by Chinese consultancy iResearch, China had more than 200 million online anime users in 2018, with nearly 80 per cent of 803 surveyed anime consumers expressing a preference for Japanese animation. Yet, for many young Chinese like Huang, an interest in Japanese pop culture does not mean an embrace of Japan as a whole. news_items.title_en: Why more Japanese women are choosing ‘silver divorce’ after decades of marriage | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: As children leave home and with changing pension rules, more older Japanese women are choosing to walk away from distant marriages.
news_items.body: Ayumi lives alone in a spacious suburban house originally bought to raise a family, her two cats now her only full-time companions. Her two daughters have grown up and left home, and her husband of more than two decades moved out nearly a year ago as they finalise a divorce. For the 62-year-old Kawasaki resident, who spoke on condition that her surname be withheld, this was not how she envisioned her later years. “He worked very long hours, including on weekends, and I was always busy taking care of the house and raising the children,” Ayumi said. “I think we worked well as a team at the beginning, but somewhere along the way, we just stopped talking like we had before.” The marriage had its fair share of ups and downs – financial stress during their daughters’ university years and the deaths of their respective parents. But the final break came when the girls left home. “It felt like we were almost strangers with nothing in common,” she said. “Before, we had always put our children first. But suddenly they had their own lives, and we both realised there was not much holding us together any more.” Ayumi’s experience reflects a growing trend across Japan. While total divorces nationwide have steadily declined since peaking in the early 2000s, separations among couples married for 20 years or longer – commonly called “silver divorce” – continue to rise. Data from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare released in September showed that such late-life break-ups reached a record 24.2 per cent in 2025, rising 0.4 percentage points from the previous year. The total number of divorces in 2025, however, fell to 179,073, down 6,831 from 185,904 in 2024. Financial independence Several changes have caused older women to re-evaluate unhappy or distant marriages later in life. Sumie Kawakami, a lecturer at Yamanashi Gakuin University and author of a book on gender issues, said an “empty nest” frequently exposed deep emotional divides built up over decades. “Many find that they had grown a long way apart during the years of raising their children,” Kawakami said. This has been exacerbated by more women entering employment, earning a wage that gives a degree of self-sufficiency previous generations lacked. A key turning point was Japan’s 2007 pension system reform, which allowed divorced spouses to claim up to 50 per cent of the Employees’ Pension Insurance contributions accumulated by their partner during the marriage. “For women earning less than 1.3 million yen [US$8,217] a year, this was significant,” Kawakami said, as it provided a financial safety net upon retirement that previously did not exist. Married, but living apart Japan’s demanding corporate culture also plays a key role long before divorce papers are filed. Under the common practice of tanshin funin (solo work transfers), companies can relocate married male employees to distant domestic or overseas offices for years at a time. Wives often stay behind so children do not have to change schools. “These situations can go on for decades,” Kawakami said. “One of my friends never actually lived in the house he bought for his family; his wife and children live there and he visits when he can. So it is not at all surprising that when the husband reaches retirement age he has nothing in common any more with his wife.” The price of silence Beyond the legal and financial costs, late-life separation can carry a distinct psychological burden. news_items.summary_en: Colombo’s luxury property rally is drawing fresh interest from Chinese-backed developments, but analysts warn against speculative excess.
news_items.body: A Chinese developer behind one of Sri Lanka’s biggest projects has reason to celebrate as a luxury property boom lifts sentiment in the South Asian nation and fuels optimism about the market’s prospects. Analysts, however, cautioned that a string of disappointing Chinese overseas property investments over the past decade underlined the risks of speculative excess that could lead to a boom-to-bust scenario, particularly in a country where regulation remained uneven. “Chinese developers, having already learned a hard lesson from the property market [slump in China], need to stay cautious,” said Wang Feng, chairman of Shanghai-based financial services group Ye Lang Capital. “I bet they won’t get carried away by the recent price surge in Sri Lanka because of their high risk-awareness.” Three new luxury residential projects in Colombo Port City – a landmark development built on reclaimed land by China Harbour Engineering Co (Chec) and the Sri Lankan government – had drawn strong interest from local buyers attracted by projections of substantial investment returns, according to a report by online magazine The Diplomat. The three developments, built by Sri Lanka’s top real estate firms, represent a combined investment of US$650 million. Developers had marketed the developments with projected returns of up to 100 per cent over four years, according to the report. Colombo Port City itself is a US$1.4 billion development being built by Chec, a unit of Chinese multinational engineering and construction company China Communications Construction. Construction began in September 2014 and it was described by China’s State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission as the largest foreign direct investment-backed infrastructure project in Sri Lanka at the time. The reclaimed land was envisioned to create a new central business district focused on tourism, financial services and logistics, eventually attracting 280,000 residents and workers, according to the state-assets regulator. In May, Chec held a topping-out ceremony for an affordable public housing project in Colombo that is expected to deliver an initial 112 homes for low-income residents, with a further 1,884 units planned. A survey by Sri Lanka’s central bank found that more than 20 per cent of flats were bought for investment purposes in the first quarter of 2026, while developers continued to shift to higher-end projects to capitalise on rising demand. About 52 per cent of home sales in the three months ended March were priced above 50 million rupees (US$150,600), up from 33 per cent a year earlier, according to the survey. Sri Lanka is among the countries participating in China’s Belt and Road Initiative, launched by President Xi Jinping in 2013 to strengthen trade and infrastructure links across Asia, Africa, Europe and beyond. Despite the optimism, questions remain about market oversight. According to The Diplomat, Sri Lanka’s Condominium Management Authority oversees the country’s luxury homes. But its main responsibility lies in monitoring and supervising completed buildings, and it has limited ability to regulate the fast-moving presale home market, where speculative capital has poured into projects. news_items.summary_en: Youth group attributes increase to heightened mental health awareness, but also students struggling to distinguish jokes from bullying.
news_items.body: Hong Kong schools handled an average of 496 bullying cases each academic year from 2022 to 2025 – a 32 per cent jump compared with the previous three years, according to the Education Bureau. A youth group attributed the increase to greater reporting driven by heightened mental health awareness, but also students struggling to distinguish playful jokes from bullying. According to the bureau, public primary and secondary schools recorded an average of 496 bullying cases each year between 2022 and 2025, up 32 per cent from the 377 recorded annually from 2019 to 2022. The bureau told the Legislative Council in 2023 that the number of cases involving school bullying, including cyberbullying, from the 2019-20 to 2021-22 school years was 411, 306 and 413 respectively. The average number for these three school years was 377. The figures were based on information contained in the bureau’s annual questionnaire surveys on guidance and discipline cases in schools. The bureau did not provide any annual breakdown for the years between 2022 and 2025. It said the data for the current school year was still being compiled. “The number of student cases involving school bullying, including cyberbullying, handled by schools averaged 496 per year between the 2022–23 and 2024–25 school years, with the annual figures remaining generally stable,” a bureau spokesman said. But he said comparing the two sets of figures for 2019–22 and 2022–25 might not be appropriate, as the first triennium was marked by the Covid pandemic, during which students attended some classes online. Last month, the Programme for International Student Assessment, a worldwide study of 15-year-olds’ learning and education by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) revealed that 22.2 per cent of students in Hong Kong aged 15 reported experiencing some form of bullying at least a few times a month. The city’s overall figure was higher than the OECD average of 19.6 per cent. Hong Kong ranked 32nd among the 86 surveyed countries and cities, including ones that were not members of the organisation. The Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups has been commissioned by the bureau to provide advice and counselling services on peer conflict management to students and parents at all primary and secondary schools this academic year. The group also has social workers stationed in 59 primary and secondary schools. Chan added that younger generations often struggled to distinguish playful joking from bullying, such as creating altered images targeting victims or repeatedly kicking classmates out of chat groups. He said resolving cases had become significantly more difficult with some students airing their grievances on social media and drawing comments from other online users. “The victim faces severe public scrutiny and media pressure, making mediated resolutions far harder to achieve,” he said. Chan noted that some cases became more complicated because victims might turn into bullies themselves when seeking revenge, making it harder for teachers and social workers to determine fault or mediate effectively. news_items.body: Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces. Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies disclose security incidents as AI systems become more capable and autonomous. Shanmugam, coordinating minister for national security, said during a speech at Singapore International Cyber Week on October 13. “We will not need to develop our own AI models for every use case. The US technology firm signed an agreement with Singapore on the sidelines of the summit, setting out areas of AI cooperation, including safety, security, responsible adoption and research into the impact of adoption. “Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Anthropic co-founder Benjamin Mann at the signing on October 13, a day before the firm opened its fifth Asia-Pacific office in the city state. Anthropic already has offices in Japan, India, South Korea and Australia. “With this [memorandum of understanding], we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world,” Mann said. news_items.title_en: Do you have empty nest syndrome? 5 signs – and expert ways to cope | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Watching your children leave home triggers a wave of mixed emotions. An expert shares how to process the shift and move forward.
news_items.body: If you feel lost or overwhelmed now your children have left the nest, you are far from alone. Many parents experience empty nest syndrome at this time of the year. “Empty nest syndrome isn’t a mental health condition, but a set of feelings or symptoms that parents might feel when all their children have left home,” says Dr Elizabeth Wakeland, consultant, clinical and forensic psychologist at Cygnet Health Care in the UK. “It’s a period of significant life change where parents are trying to figure out who they are and what their life looks like now their children are no longer in the home.” Empty nest symptoms Here are five signs of empty nest syndrome to look out for and advice about how to navigate this period. 1. Sense of grief “Some parents might experience emotions around grief, loss and sadness,” Wakeland says. “Although their children haven’t passed away, there’s still a loss of presence and a change in relationship.” 2. Anxiety “There might also be some feelings of anxiety,” Wakeland says. “Children living outside the home might increase your anxiety because they are no longer with you all the time and you might be worried about their safety.” That anxiety might manifest itself in constant communication. “This anxiety might present in behaviours that are directly related, such as calling or sending messages constantly to check in on your children,” she says. “This is when our involvement, or what people sometimes refer to as ‘helicopter parenting’, might come into play.” 3. Mood changes “As well as these low feelings and a sense of emptiness, there might also be some positive feelings,” Wakeland says. “For example, you might have some excitement about your child moving on and progressing, or some pride in what they are going on to do. “So, it might feel a bit up and down for a while, and a mixture of positive and negative emotions might play out.” This can trigger guilt: “A parent might feel guilt around how they should or shouldn’t feel, or what they should or shouldn’t be doing now that their children have moved out.” 4. Identity crisis “When you become a parent you have to adapt and mould yourself and your life around your children,” Wakeland says. “Children take up a lot of time, energy and thinking, and it becomes a big part of your identity. Therefore, many parents experience a bit of an identity crisis when their children leave home. “It can provoke questions such as, ‘Who am I? What should I do with my time now?’ It’s a big shift.” 5. Loneliness “It’s wonderful to see children moving on and progressing, but it can make parents feel left behind or feel like they are not part of their child’s new world,” she says. “As their child steps into their new social life and immerses themselves into university life, parents are forced to take a back seat.” This can be particularly challenging for single parents. “If you are going through this alone as a single parent, those feelings of loneliness and loss can feel even more heightened because now it’s just you left in the house,” Wakeland says. Be kind to yourself “It’s really normal to feel like this and it’s OK to feel happy and sad at the prospect of your children moving on,” Wakeland says. “The emotions will change and fluctuate, so don’t be too hard on yourself about it. news_items.summary_en: The former US president slammed his successor’s ‘corruption and incompetence’ and blamed his ‘bad decisions’ for the rising cost of living.
news_items.body: Former US president Barack Obama delivered a scathing critique of his successor, Donald Trump, at a rally in Ohio on Saturday to support Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,’” Obama declared in Cleveland. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.” The 65-year-old Democrat blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, a top voter concern amid soaring fuel prices. “The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said. “Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for.” He noted that instead of lowering costs, the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn. “I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation,” Obama said. “He should be on HGTV.” He went on: “There’s gold everywhere. He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Obama also urged voters to cast their ballots as soon as possible since early voting is already open in this northern industrial state. “Don’t procrastinate, don’t equivocate,” Obama said. The former president retains considerable popularity among the Democratic base, which he is keen to leverage to support his party’s candidates in the crucial coming elections that will decide control of Congress. In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown will attempt a comeback against incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, while the race for governor will be contested between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate in 2024. Polls for Ohio give Democrats a slight lead in both those races, but the results are expected to be close. Nationally, polls also suggest that Democrats could regain control of the House of Representatives but face a much more competitive contest for the Senate. After Cleveland, Obama will head north to Michigan this evening for a rally in Detroit alongside Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate.
