news_items.title_en: In Focus | China’s next generation of leaders waiting in the wings for more senior roles | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: A meeting in Beijing this week will lay the groundwork for members of the Communist Party’s seventh generation – or 7G – to take on key roles.
news_items.body: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the fourth part of this series, William Zheng looks at how the next generation of the party is being formed. When China’s political elites gather behind closed doors in Beijing for the Communist Party’s fifth plenum on Monday, much of the attention will be on the quiet preparations for allocating hundreds of pivotal roles in next year’s 21st party congress. At the heart of this transition is the rise of the party’s seventh generation – often referred to as the 7G – who were born in the late 1960s and the 1970s and whose ascent will be critical in shaping China’s political trajectory. Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at Tsinghua University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies, said the party was looking for cadres who had “absolute political loyalty, integrity, fighting spirit, technological or ‘hard science’ expertise, grass-roots experience and hardship resilience”. “Just like their predecessors, they must demonstrate unquestioned loyalty and integrity. But given China’s technological advancement into uncharted areas, the new leaders will have to know emerging technology and hard science as China can no longer copy from others.” However, recent patterns within the party suggest that Beijing is giving age less weight when it comes to promotions, while the far-reaching anti-corruption campaign is hitting this generation as hard as any other. The 7G Regardless of whether Xi Jinping, now 73, chooses to stay in charge beyond the 2032 party congress, he will still need a deep bench of loyal and talented younger officials to carry out his policies. In recent decades, candidates for Politburo seats have usually been identified many years ahead. Most candidates for membership of the key decision-making body in 2032 will currently be members of the party’s Central Committee or will be selected as alternate members at next year’s party congress. Traditionally, most Central Committee members, who have a ministerial-level rank, are required to step down at the age of 65. Meanwhile, Politburo members observe an informal rule known as “seven up, eight down”, in which those under the age of 67 may serve another five-year term, while those aged 68 or older must retire. Xi broke these precedents for some key figures in 2022, including top diplomat Wang Yi, then aged 69, who was seen as indispensable for managing China’s foreign relations amid escalating competition with the United States. He also kept the country’s top general Zhang Youxia, then aged 72, in place to manage the country’s military modernisation programme, but Zhang later fell from favour and was detained earlier this year on suspicion of corruption. Roughly two-thirds of the current Central Committee will have reached the statutory retirement age by the time of the party congress in October next year. Consequently, the seventh generation, currently about 8 per cent of the party’s central leadership body, is expected to become the biggest cohort. Only 7G officials who are already members of the Central Committee or those who have been newly appointed as ministers and provincial leaders – who will get their Central Committee seat in 2027 – are likely candidates for leadership roles beyond 2032. The leading candidates Some of these contenders have already taken over top regional and ministerial roles this year. They include Zhu Zhongming, born in April 1972, who was appointed as mayor of Shanghai late last month, a role that puts him in line to become the city’s next party chief. Zhu, 54, is a career finance official who spent much of his working life in his native province of Zhejiang, where he worked under Premier Li Qiang while he was governor. The Houthis’ Al-Masirah outlet reported a series of “Saudi enemy air strikes” targeting Sanaa, including one on a house that killed at least four people and wounded several others. A separate strike at a residence building for cement factory workers in the Sanaa governorate killed six women and one child and wounded three others, the broadcaster said. Yemen’s civil war, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis against the Saudi-supported and internationally recognised government, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022, but erupted again in July as the wider Middle East war roiled the region. The strikes in Yemen came after the Saudi-led coalition announced it had intercepted two missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif and Yanbu, in the kingdom’s west. Earlier, Riyadh’s civil defence agency broadcast warnings of “potential danger” for four western regions, including Taif and Yanbu as well Mecca, home to Islam’s holiest city, and Yanbu. The alerts were all rescinded minutes later.

news_items.title_en: China’s J-20 stealth jet designers plan to put powerful radar into aircraft wing | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Military aircraft designers propose a wing-mounted early-warning radar to expand coverage during air combat.
news_items.body: Fighter jets typically house their main radars behind a radome in the nose, while conventional airborne early-warning aircraft often carry large radar arrays in prominent structures above the fuselage. Although aircraft wings offer a large surface area, their relatively thin cross-sections leave limited internal space for radar equipment. Top Chinese military aircraft designers have now proposed a revolutionary method to integrate large antenna arrays into aircraft wings, using flight manoeuvres and coordinated formations of unmanned aircraft to expand radar coverage. The design was outlined in a study published online on October 10 in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Measurement & Control Technology, which presented wing-mounted radar as a new approach to building multifunctional, high-performance airborne early-warning systems. “Wing-mounted early-warning radar is a new type of mission payload designed to meet the early-warning needs of distributed air combat,” researcher Ren Yunsong and his team wrote, describing the concept as “a new pathway” to developing systems with strong detection capabilities. Ren and his team are affiliated with AVIC Chengdu Aircraft Design and Research Institute, which developed China’s J-20 stealth fighter and was identified by the country’s defence ministry as the designer of the two-seat J-20S, a variant intended to operate alongside unmanned aircraft. The concept builds on distributed air combat, a strategic idea first proposed by the US Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency or Darpa in 2014 to explore future air warfare. The researchers argued that this approach could not rely solely on conventional early-warning aircraft, which use large radar arrays and high-power systems, but would instead require numerous smaller, lower-cost unmanned aircraft to work together to provide surveillance. This creates a technical challenge: achieving large-scale detection capabilities with relatively small individual platforms. The proposed design integrates the antenna array, control components and associated systems within the wing structure, with the radiating surface facing downwards and a protective cover following the aircraft’s outer contours, increasing the available antenna aperture without requiring a large external radar dome. To direct the radar towards different sectors, the researchers propose changing the aircraft’s flight attitude. In the proposed side-flying mode, an unmanned aircraft rolls at an angle of more than 45 degrees, tilting the wing-mounted array from a downward-facing position towards the side. “By adjusting the drone’s flight attitude, the radar beam can be dynamically controlled, expanding the airspace covered by early warning,” Ren wrote. The design is intended to support distributed airborne early-warning operations, in which multiple smaller unmanned aircraft share surveillance duties rather than relying on a single large platform. “The research provides a reusable and verifiable design paradigm for the engineering implementation of wing warning radars and has a promising application prospect and promotion value,” Ren’s team wrote. The paper proposes four operating modes, including all-direction and multi-direction detection, as well as coordinated operations in which aircraft provide wide-area coverage, concentrate on specific targets or work together to counter electronic interference. “Cooperative detection by multiple aircraft is a core enabling technology for the operational concept of ‘small platforms, big capabilities’,” it said. The researchers said the approach could provide early-warning capabilities approaching or exceeding those of conventional early-warning aircraft without relying on large platforms. Ren said the design would provide a solid information-sensing foundation for distributed air combat involving next-generation aircraft. news_items.title_en: Longevity-first healthcare takes spotlight at Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: The event explores innovative breakthroughs and policies emphasising prediction and prevention to help people lead longer, healthier lives.
news_items.body: Issues affecting ageing populations worldwide will form the core of discussions for policymakers and health industry leaders gathered at the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit, with a particular emphasis on how practising prediction and prevention can help ensure life is lived to its fullest. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has positioned itself as a global leader in transformative healthcare policy, and Dr Asma Al Mannaei, executive director of the health life science sector at the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi, regards the summit as an opportunity to share how those policies are playing out in real time. “Precision medicine is at the heart of it,” Al Mannaei explains, adding that the key to ensuring better health is “understanding each person’s risk through their genome, their biomarkers and their daily life, then acting early.” The Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit is the flagship event of the Future Health platform, the UAE capital’s year-round initiative to promote global collaboration and transformative health innovation. The stated goal of the summit is to shape a future where innovation and collaboration come together “to enable longer, healthier lives for all”. Much of the summit will be focused on the world’s ageing populations – a common denominator between contemporary societies, with the World Health Organization estimating that by 2050, there will be more than 2 billion people aged over 60 across the globe. This statistic has not only drawn more attention to the issue of how to care for people as they age, but Al Mannaei also points out that it has created a need to design entire health systems focused on ensuring the advancing years are spent in as much good health as possible. “Every health system faces the same question: will those added years be healthy years? Our answer is to invest now in prediction and prevention,” she says. “Our model has four steps: we sense, we predict, we prevent and we personalise. We sense through genomics, screening and data. We predict risk years before the symptoms appear. And we prevent through early targeted intervention.” Among Abu Dhabi’s success stories is the Emirati Genome Programme (EGP), launched across the UAE in 2019 with a target of mapping the genetic make-up of all Emiratis. To date, more than 800,000 records have been collected. Al Mannaei says the idea behind the programme is that knowing an individual’s genetic make-up can help establish a “foundation for precision prevention”. Already, the EGP data has proved revelatory. For example, it revealed that within the Emirati population, there are around 100 genetic factors associated with inherited vision loss. Other initiatives include Malaffi, the region’s first health information exchange that is a strategic initiative of the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi. Launched in 2019 and operated by Abu Dhabi Health Data Services, Malaffi connects more than 3,000 healthcare facilities and brings together over 4 billion records for more than 14 million patients. “It gives clinicians secure access to patients’ comprehensive health records, supporting continuity of care, patient safety and better-informed clinical decisions,” Al Mannaei says. “In Abu Dhabi, policy, regulation, care delivery, research, technology and investment move together around one vision,” she notes. “When we built the Emirati Genome Programme, we built the governance, the data, the infrastructure and the partnership at the same time. That let discovery move into care and into the economy at speed.” Al Mannaei adds: “I hope Abu Dhabi will be known as the place that proved a longevity-first health system works. It will be the blueprint of how health systems can sense, predict, prevent and personalise, helping people everywhere live longer, healthier and more fulfilling lives.” Watch the video for more insights from Dr Asma Al Mannaei about Abu Dhabi’s role in advancing healthcare focused on longevity.
